yehud-medinata.t: Yehud Medinata, the small Persian province of Judah centred on Jerusalem's rebuilt temple, where Second Temple Judaism took shape.
yehud-medinata.o: After Cyrus of the Achaemenid Empire conquered Babylon in 539 BCE, Judaean exiles were allowed to return to Jerusalem. The province of Yehud was formed in the hills around the city, and under the governor Zerubbabel the Second Temple was completed c. 515 BCE.
yehud-medinata.r: Persian-appointed governors and the high priests of the temple shared authority. Nehemiah, a court official, rebuilt Jerusalem's walls c. 445 BCE, and Ezra brought the law of Moses to the centre of community life. The province minted small silver coins inscribed Yehud and used Aramaic for administration.
yehud-medinata.e: Yehud passed peacefully to Alexander of the Macedonian Empire in 332 BCE and then to the Ptolemaic Empire and the Seleucid Empire. The texts and institutions shaped there formed the basis of later Judaism.

yufirid-dynasty.t: A highland Yemeni dynasty of the Himyarite tribe of Hiwal that held Sanaa and Shibam for over a century under nominal Abbasid rule.
yufirid-dynasty.o: Yu'fir ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Hiwali, from a Himyarite family, seized the highland fortress of Shibam Kawkaban around 847 and soon controlled Sanaa, ousting Abbasid governors while still naming the caliph in Friday prayers.
yufirid-dynasty.r: The Yufirids ruled a tribal highland state from Shibam and Sanaa, a rival to the Ziyadid dynasty in the coastal Tihama. They faced the arrival of the Zaydi imam al-Hadi in the north in 897 and the Isma'ili missionaries Ali ibn al-Fadl and Ibn Hawshab, who briefly captured Sanaa. As'ad ibn Ibrahim recovered the city and dominated highland politics in the early 10th century.
yufirid-dynasty.e: After As'ad's death in 944 the dynasty weakened through family feuds and tribal revolts. By about 997 it had lost Sanaa, and the highlands were contested between Zaydi imams, local chiefs and later the Sulayhid dynasty.

yuezhi.t: Nomads of the Gansu corridor who, driven west by the Xiongnu, conquered Bactria and gave rise to the Kushan Empire.
yuezhi.o: Chinese sources describe the Yuezhi as a powerful pastoral people between Dunhuang and the Qilian Mountains in the 3rd century BCE, strong enough to hold the young Xiongnu leader Modu as a hostage. Around 176 BCE the Xiongnu defeated them, and their king was later killed and his skull made into a drinking cup.
yuezhi.r: The main body, the Greater Yuezhi, migrated west through the Ili valley, displacing the Saka, then were pushed on by the Wusun to the Amu Darya. When the Han envoy Zhang Qian visited about 128 BCE they ruled Bactria from north of the river, governing through five xihou or princely chiefdoms. Their identification with the Tocharian-speaking peoples is widely held but debated.
yuezhi.e: In the 1st century CE Kujula Kadphises, chief of the Guishuang (Kushan) branch, united the five chiefdoms and founded the Kushan Empire. The Lesser Yuezhi who stayed behind in the Qilian Mountains merged with the Qiang peoples.

ychsma.t: A coastal lordship of the Rímac and Lurín valleys centred on Pachacamac, the most famous oracle and pilgrimage site of the ancient Andes.
ychsma.o: Ychsma, or Ichma, emerged around 1100 in the Lurín and lower Rímac valleys, where modern Lima stands, after the decline of Wari influence. It took over Pachacamac, a sacred site occupied since the time of the Lima culture, and made it the heart of its territory.
ychsma.r: Ychsma was a group of lordships united around the cult of Pachacamac, the creator god whose oracle drew pilgrims from across the Andes. Its lords built a series of pyramids with ramps at Pachacamac and other sites such as Armatambo and Mateo Salado. The economy relied on irrigation canals drawn from the Rímac and on fishing.
ychsma.e: The Incas absorbed Ychsma peacefully around 1470 and respected Pachacamac, adding a Temple of the Sun and an Acllahuasi. In 1533 Hernando Pizarro looted the temple. Spanish Lima was founded in Ychsma territory in 1535, and Pachacamac is now a major archaeological site.

yamhad.t: Yamhad, the Amorite great kingdom of Aleppo, which dominated northern Syria in the 18th and 17th centuries BCE until the Hittites destroyed it.
yamhad.o: Sumu-epuh founded the kingdom at Halab, modern Aleppo, around 1810 BCE. He resisted Shamshi-Adad's Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia, and his son Yarim-Lim I made Yamhad the leading power of Syria, allied with Mari and Babylon; a Mari letter claims twenty kings followed him.
yamhad.r: Its great kings ruled through dependent kingdoms such as Alalakh in the Kingdom of Mukish and Ebla, and their prestige rested on the temple of the storm god Hadad on the Aleppo citadel. Wealth came from the trade between the Euphrates and the Mediterranean, and Hurrian culture spread widely among the elite.
yamhad.e: Hattusili I of the Hittite Empire attacked Yamhad, and Mursili I destroyed Aleppo c. 1595 BCE. A reduced kingdom survived until the Mitanni Empire absorbed it in the 16th century BCE. The Aleppo storm-god temple remained venerated for centuries.
